Neonatal Cyanosis

Author: Jules Atkins, RMSupplied by: Brandi Catt, Attribution, via Wikimedia Commons · Cornelia Csuk, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

Cyanosis Definition & Types

  • Bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes
  • It is on two types: peripheral and central

Peripheral cyanosis is bluish discoloration of distal extremities (hands and feet of the neonate) while the rest of the body is normal in color (pink to white)

Peripheral cyanosis in newborn for the first 2 days is normal and it is called acrocyanosis and it occurs due to immature control of vascular tone in newborns (vessels in extremities stay dilated, which lead to vascular congestion and bluish discoloration)

The second type of cyanosis is the central cyanosis, it is bluish discoloration of the entire body, especially tongue, mucous membranes and trunk

Central cyanosis is caused by increase the amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the newborn blood

Central cyanosis in newborn is normal for the first 5-10 minutes after birth, if it persist then it requires immediate evaluation because it reflects serious underlying condition that has to be managed fast

Central Cyanosis Pathophysiology

Cyanosis occurs due to increase the amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the blood due to many causes (will be explained a little later)

Cyanosis become evident at ≥ 3 g/dl of deoxygenated hemoglobin in the neonate blood

If you ask at which oxygen saturation this occurs? It is variable

meg and rahul, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

There is no specific oxygen saturation you would see cyanosis at, because cyanosis depends on amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin

E.g. if the infant has hemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dl, their oxygen saturation has to reach to less than 70% to develop clinical cyanosis (30% of 10 g/dl is 3 g/dl which is the concentration of deoxygenated hemoglobin needed for clinical cyanosis to develop), if the infant hemoglobin conc is 20 g/dl, their oxygen saturation has to reach below 85% for them to develop clinical cyanosis (15% of 20g/dl 3 g/dl)

There is 5 possible scenarios for deoxygenated hemoglobin to increase (thus leading to cyanosis)

Hypoventilation: Asphyxia

V/Q mismatch: PPHN

Diffusion abnormalities: MAS

Oxygen transport: Methemoglobinemia

Heart problems: TGA

Central Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis

Wide differential diagnosis including:

Hypoglycemia

Sepsis: second most common cause

CVS (third most common cause)

Cyanotic congenital heart diseases: TGA, TOF, truncus arteriosus … => should be identified quickly

Heart failure due to sepsis, myocarditis, SVT, heart block…

RS

RDS: surfactant deficiency (first most common cause)

Transient tachypnea of newborn: self limiting

Meconium aspiration: impairs oxygen diffusion

Diaphragmatic hernia

Pneumothorax

Pneumonia

Persistent pulmonary hypertension

Nervous system

Asphyxia

Intracranial hemorrhage

Neuromuscular disease

Maternal sedative drugs

Meningitis

Blood

Blood loss

Polycythemia

Methemoglobinemia

Peripheral Cyanosis Differential Diagnosis

There is specific differential diagnosis for peripheral cyanosis if it persists for more than 24 hours:

Sepsis

Cardiogenic shock

Hypovolemia

Exposure to cold air or water

What do you do if neonate has central cyanosis on examination

Check ABCs and check vitals

If oxygen saturation is less than 95% then administer supplemental oxygen

Assess for signs of respiratory distress: nasal flaring, chest retractions, tachypnea (more than 60 breaths/min), stridor and grunting, if those are seen on the baby then think of differentials related to respiratory system

If neonate has weak, irregular or absent respirations then think of differential diagnoses related to heart and nervous system

Hyperoxia test differentiate between cardiac and non cardiac causes of cyanosis (100% oxygen is supplied for neonate for 10 minutes, and their oxygen saturation is checked after, if their saturation increases substantially then the cause pulmonary or CNS related, if their saturation still same then cardiac)

Take full history from mother (pregnancy history, birth history, medical history)

Do complete physical examination of the neonate

Management

After checking ABCs, Neonate may need respiratory support in form of bag mask ventilation or intubation

Send for CBC (check for anemia and lymphocytosis), blood cultures looking for sepsis, blood glucose looking for hypoglycemia

Send for chest x ray looking for pneumothorax, heart failure

ECG and echocardiogram looking for congenital heart diseases

Manage accordingly
